source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 2 (PDF 22-53, printed 19-50); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 2 (Force and Motion), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The total distance travelled by a body is an example of a:
blocks.explanation: Total distance travelled is a scalar; it needs only magnitude (2.1).

book_ref.quote: calculating the total distance travelled (scalar)

blocks.prompt: 2 Scalars are physical quantities that are described by:
blocks.explanation: A scalar is described solely by a magnitude, with no mention of direction (2.1).

book_ref.quote: Scalars are physical quantities that are described solely by a magnitude

blocks.prompt: 3 A scalar quantity can be fully characterized by:

options.text: a single number and its unit
a number and a direction only

blocks.explanation: Scalars are directionless and are fully given by a single number with its unit (2.1).

book_ref.quote: fully characterized by a single number and its associated unit

blocks.prompt: 4 Which one of the following is a scalar quantity?
blocks.explanation: Speed, the rate of covering distance, is listed among scalars (2.1); velocity, displacement and force are vectors (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Speed: The rate at which an object covers distance.

blocks.prompt: 5 Temperature is a measure of the:

options.text: average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
total momentum of particles in a substance

blocks.explanation: The chapter defines temperature as a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles (2.1).

book_ref.quote: Temperature: A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.

blocks.prompt: 6 Which pair consists of scalar quantities only?
blocks.explanation: Energy and time are both in the chapter's list of scalars (2.1); force, acceleration and velocity are vectors (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Energy: The capacity to do work.

blocks.prompt: 7 Physical quantities that need both magnitude and direction for their complete specification are called:
blocks.explanation: Vectors have magnitude as well as direction for their complete specification (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Those physical quantities which have magnitude well as direction for their complete specification.

blocks.prompt: 8 The change in position of an object is called:
blocks.explanation: Displacement is the change in position of an object; it has magnitude and direction, e.g. 10 m towards west (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Displacement: The change in position of an object.

blocks.prompt: 9 Acceleration is produced in a body when its velocity changes in:
blocks.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which may occur in speed or direction or both (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Acceleration: The rate of change of velocity that occurs in either speed or direction or both

blocks.prompt: 10 In a vector diagram, the length of the arrow represents the vector's:
blocks.explanation: The length of the arrow gives the magnitude and its head shows the direction (2.2).

book_ref.quote: The length of the arrows indicates the magnitude

blocks.prompt: 11 In print, a vector is usually denoted by:

options.text: a bold face letter or an arrow head above the symbol
an italic letter with a dot above it

blocks.explanation: Vectors are denoted by bold face letters (V, F) or by an arrow head above the symbol (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Vectors are typically denoted by bold face letters

blocks.prompt: 12 The effective value of a vector in a given direction is called its:
blocks.explanation: A component of a vector is its effective value in a given direction (2.2).

book_ref.quote: A component of a vector is its effective value in a given direction.

blocks.prompt: 13 Components of a vector along mutually perpendicular directions are called:
blocks.explanation: Components along mutually perpendicular directions are called rectangular components (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Such components are called rectangular components.

blocks.prompt: 14 A vector A makes an angle θ with the x-axis. Its x-component is:
blocks.explanation: From the right-angled triangle OMP, Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ (Eqs. 2.2, 2.3).

book_ref.quote: Considering the right angled triangle OMP

blocks.prompt: 15 A force of 20 N acts at 30° to the x-axis. Its y-component is:
blocks.explanation: Fy = F sin θ = 20 N × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N (Eq. 2.3). 17.3 N is the x-component.

book_ref.quote: the magnitude of A⃗y or y-component of A⃗ is:

blocks.prompt: 16 A force of 20 N acts at 30° to the x-axis. Its x-component is:

book_ref.quote: Considering the right angled triangle OMP, the magnitude of A⃗x

blocks.prompt: 17 The rectangular components of a vector are Ax = 6 units and Ay = 8 units. Its magnitude is:

book_ref.quote: we can find out the magnitude of the vector by using Pythagorean Theorem

blocks.prompt: 18 For the vector with Ax = 6 units and Ay = 8 units, the angle with the x-axis is about:

book_ref.quote: The direction θ is given by

blocks.prompt: 19 Two forces of equal magnitude F have a resultant of magnitude √3 F. The angle between them is:
blocks.explanation: As in Example 2.1: R² = (F + F cos θ)² + (F sin θ)² = 2F² + 2F² cos θ. With R² = 3F², cos θ = 0.5, so θ = 60°.

book_ref.quote: Find the angle between two forces of equal magnitude

blocks.prompt: 20 The angle between the two rectangular components of a vector is:
blocks.explanation: Rectangular components are at right angles to each other (2.2).

book_ref.quote: Since these are at right angle to each other

blocks.prompt: 21 If the product of two vectors results in a vector quantity, the product is called:
blocks.explanation: A product giving a scalar is a scalar product; one giving a vector is a vector product (2.3).

book_ref.quote: if the product of two vectors results in a vector quantity then it is called vector product

blocks.prompt: 22 The scalar product of A and B is defined as:
blocks.explanation: A.B = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors (Eq. 2.6).

book_ref.quote: where A and B are the magnitudes of vectors A⃗ and B⃗ and θ is the angle between them

blocks.prompt: 23 Physically, A.B equals A multiplied by:

options.text: the projection of A on B
the projection of B on A
the component of B perpendicular to A

blocks.explanation: A.B = A (projection of B on A) = A(B cos θ) (2.3, Fig. 2.2).

book_ref.quote: these are first brought to a common origin

blocks.prompt: 24 A force of 50 N moves its point of application 10 m in a direction at 60° to the force. The work done is:
blocks.explanation: Work = F.d = Fd cos θ = 50 N × 10 m × cos 60° = 250 J (2.3).

book_ref.quote: We come across this type of product when we consider the work done by a force

blocks.prompt: 25 Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 5 units make an angle of 60°. Their scalar product is:
blocks.explanation: A.B = AB cos θ = 4 × 5 × cos 60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 units (Eq. 2.6).

book_ref.quote: The scalar product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ is written as A⃗.B⃗

blocks.prompt: 26 Since A.B = B.A, the scalar product is:
blocks.explanation: The order of multiplication is irrelevant, so the scalar product is commutative (2.3).

book_ref.quote: The order of multiplication is irrelevant.

blocks.prompt: 27 The scalar product of two mutually perpendicular vectors is:

book_ref.quote: The scalar product of two mutually perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°) is zero.

blocks.prompt: 28 For two antiparallel vectors A and B, the scalar product is:

book_ref.quote: For antiparallel vectors (θ = 180°)

blocks.prompt: 29 The self product A.A of a vector is equal to:
blocks.explanation: A.A = AA cos 0° = A², the square of its magnitude (2.3).

book_ref.quote: The self product of a vector A⃗ is equal to square of its magnitude.

blocks.prompt: 30 Two parallel vectors have magnitudes 3 units and 7 units. Their scalar product is:
blocks.explanation: For parallel vectors θ = 0°, so A.B = AB cos 0° = 3 × 7 = 21 units (2.3). -21 units would be for antiparallel vectors.

book_ref.quote: The scalar product of two parallel vectors is equal to the product of their magnitudes.

blocks.prompt: 31 Two vectors have rectangular components Ax = 3, Ay = 4, Az = 0 and Bx = 4, By = -3, Bz = 0. The angle between them is:
blocks.explanation: A.B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz = 12 - 12 + 0 = 0, so cos θ = 0 and θ = 90° (Eqs. 2.7, 2.8).

book_ref.quote: Scalar product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ in terms of their rectangular components

blocks.prompt: 32 In A × B = AB sin θ n̂, the unit vector n̂ is:

options.text: perpendicular to the plane containing A and B
along the bisector of A and B

blocks.explanation: n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A and B (Eq. 2.9).

book_ref.quote: is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A⃗ and B⃗

blocks.prompt: 33 The direction of the vector product A × B is found by:

options.text: the left hand rule for scalars

blocks.explanation: The direction of the product vector is determined by the right hand rule (2.3).

book_ref.quote: Its direction can be determined by right hand rule.

blocks.prompt: 34 In the right hand rule, the first vector A is rotated into B through:

options.text: the larger of the two possible angles
the smaller of the two possible angles

blocks.explanation: Rotate A into B through the smaller angle; the erect thumb gives the direction of A × B (2.3).

book_ref.quote: through the smaller of the two possible angles

blocks.prompt: 35 Compared with A × B, the vector B × A is:

options.text: equal in magnitude but opposite in direction

blocks.explanation: By the direction rule, B × A is opposite in sign to A × B, so A × B = -B × A (Eq. 2.10).

book_ref.quote: is a vector opposite in sign to A⃗ x B⃗

blocks.prompt: 36 Because A × B ≠ B × A, the cross product is:
blocks.explanation: A × B is not the same as B × A, so the cross product is non-commutative (2.3).

book_ref.quote: the cross product is non commutative

blocks.prompt: 37 The magnitude of A × B is maximum when the angle between A and B is:
blocks.explanation: sin θ is largest at θ = 90°, so A × B = AB n̂ (2.3).

book_ref.quote: The cross product of two perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°) has maximum magnitude

blocks.prompt: 38 The cross product of a vector with itself, A × A, is:
blocks.explanation: For parallel vectors θ = 0°, so A × A = A² sin 0° n̂ = 0, a null vector (2.3).

book_ref.quote: The cross product of two parallel vectors is null vector

blocks.prompt: 39 The magnitude of A × B is equal to the:

options.text: perimeter of the parallelogram with A and B as sides
area of the parallelogram with A and B as adjacent sides
length of the diagonal of that parallelogram

blocks.explanation: |A × B| equals the area of the parallelogram formed with A and B as two adjacent sides (2.3, Fig. 2.4 d).

book_ref.quote: is equal to the area of the parallelogram formed with A⃗ and B⃗

blocks.prompt: 40 Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are vectors of 5 cm and 8 cm with 30° between them. Its area is:

book_ref.quote: As a consequence A⃗ x A⃗ = 0 (θ = 0°)

blocks.prompt: 41 Two vectors of 3 units and 4 units make an angle of 30°. The magnitude of their vector product is:
blocks.explanation: |A × B| = AB sin θ = 3 × 4 × sin 30° = 6 units (Eq. 2.9). 10.4 units would be AB cos 30°.

book_ref.quote: The vector product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗, is a vector which is defined as

blocks.prompt: 42 If |A × B| = A.B / √3, the angle between A and B is:
blocks.explanation: AB sin θ = AB cos θ / √3 gives tan θ = 1/√3, so θ = 30° (Eqs. 2.6, 2.9).

book_ref.quote: The direction of the product vector is perpendicular to this plane.

blocks.prompt: 43 The torque τ produced by a force F acting at position vector r is given by:
blocks.explanation: Torque is the vector product of r and F: τ = r × F (2.3).

book_ref.quote: the turning effect of the force called the torque

blocks.prompt: 44 The force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B is:
blocks.explanation: The magnetic force is given by the vector product of v and B: F = q(v × B) (2.3).

book_ref.quote: in a magnetic field of strength B⃗ is given by vector product

blocks.prompt: 45 A force of 20 N acts perpendicular to a position vector of 0.5 m from the axis of rotation. The magnitude of the torque is:

book_ref.quote: When a force F⃗ is applied on a rigid body at a point

blocks.prompt: 46 The equations of motion can be applied only to objects moving:

options.text: in a straight line with constant acceleration
in a circle with constant speed
in a straight line with changing acceleration
in any path with any acceleration

blocks.explanation: The equations apply only to motion in a straight line with constant acceleration (2.4).

book_ref.quote: These equations of motion can only be applied to those objects which are moving in a straight line with constant acceleration.

blocks.prompt: 47 The three kinematic variables used in the equations of motion are:
blocks.explanation: The equations describe motion in terms of velocity (v), position (s) and time (t) (2.4).

book_ref.quote: three kinematic variables: velocity (v), position (s) and time (t)

blocks.prompt: 48 The third equation of motion relates the pair:
blocks.explanation: Velocity-time, position-time and velocity-position give the first, second and third equations respectively (2.4).

book_ref.quote: In this order they are called first equation of motion, second equation of motion and third equation of motion

blocks.prompt: 49 A body moving at 5 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² for 4 s. Its final velocity is:

book_ref.quote: It correlates the final velocity attained by a body with initial velocity and the time interval t

blocks.prompt: 50 In the velocity-time graph of uniformly accelerated motion, the slope of the line gives the:
blocks.explanation: The slope BC/AC of line AB equals the acceleration a (2.4).

book_ref.quote: by taking the slope of line AB, Which is equal to acceleration a

blocks.prompt: 51 In the graphical derivation of the second equation of motion, the displacement equals the area of:

options.text: a rectangle plus a triangle under the velocity-time graph

blocks.explanation: S = area OABD = area of rectangle OACD + area of triangle ABC (2.4).

book_ref.quote: Second equation of motion can be derived using velocity-time graph

blocks.prompt: 52 When the velocity of a body is not constant, displacement is found by multiplying time with the:
blocks.explanation: Displacement = average velocity × time when the velocity is not constant (2.4).

book_ref.quote: If velocity of the body is not constant, we can use average velocity instead of velocity.

blocks.prompt: 53 A body starts at 12 m s⁻¹ and reaches 20 m s⁻¹ in 6 s with uniform acceleration. The distance covered is:

book_ref.quote: Let it covers a distance S in a particular direction during time t

blocks.prompt: 54 A car moving at 8 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. The distance it covers is:

book_ref.quote: Suppose a body is moving with uniform acceleration a along a straight line

blocks.prompt: 55 In the graphical derivation of the third equation, the area OABD under the velocity-time graph is treated as a:

options.text: trapezium: ½ (sum of parallel sides) × height

blocks.explanation: S = ½ (OA + BD) × OD, i.e. ½ (sum of parallel sides) × height (2.4).

book_ref.quote: the total distance S travelled by a body is given by the area OABD under the graph

blocks.prompt: 56 A car starts from rest and reaches 72 km h⁻¹ after covering 100 m with uniform acceleration. Its acceleration is:

book_ref.quote: Consider a body moving along a straight line with an initial velocity vi

blocks.prompt: 57 A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest by a uniform retardation of 4 m s⁻². The distance covered before stopping is:
blocks.explanation: a = -4 m s⁻² (opposite to vi). 2aS = vf² - vi²: 2(-4)S = 0 - 400, S = 50 m (Eq. 2.16).

book_ref.quote: A negative sign is assigned to quantities where direction is opposite to that of initial velocity.

blocks.prompt: 58 In solving straight-line problems with the equations of motion, the direction of the initial velocity is taken as:
blocks.explanation: Initial velocity is taken as positive; quantities opposite to it are given a negative sign (2.4).

book_ref.quote: In such cases initial velocity is taken as positive.

blocks.prompt: 59 The average value of the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is taken as:
blocks.explanation: g is taken as 9.8 m s⁻² in the downward direction (2.4).

book_ref.quote: its average value at the Earth surface is taken as 9.8 ms⁻² in the downward direction

blocks.prompt: 60 A speed of 108 km h⁻¹ expressed in m s⁻¹ is:
blocks.explanation: 108 × 1000 m / 3600 s = 30 m s⁻¹ (the conversion used in Example 2.4).

book_ref.quote: In a short distance race, a contestant in a car starts from rest

blocks.prompt: 61 A body falling freely under gravity is the most familiar example of:
blocks.explanation: Free fall is the most familiar example of uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line (2.5).

book_ref.quote: the most familiar example of uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion

blocks.prompt: 62 In vacuum, a heavy stone and a light coin are dropped together from the same height. They strike the ground with:

options.text: velocities in the ratio of their masses

blocks.explanation: All bodies fall freely in vacuum with the same acceleration g, so from the same height they strike the ground with the same velocity (2.5).

book_ref.quote: different bodies, when allowed to fall from the same height, strike the ground with the same velocity

blocks.prompt: 63 In the chapter's sign rule, g is taken negative for a body that is:
blocks.explanation: g is positive for a falling body (vi = 0) and negative for a body projected vertically upward (2.5).

book_ref.quote: negative for a body projected vertically upward

blocks.prompt: 64 A stone is dropped from rest. Its velocity after 2.5 s is:

book_ref.quote: The equations of motion for a freely falling body, on putting a = g, become

blocks.prompt: 65 A stone dropped from rest falls for 2.5 s. The distance it falls is about:

book_ref.quote: Its experimental value is 9.8 m s⁻² in SI units.

blocks.prompt: 66 A ball is dropped from a height of 122.5 m. The time it takes to reach the ground is:

book_ref.quote: This means that different bodies, when allowed to fall from the same height

blocks.prompt: 67 A ball is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹. The maximum height it reaches is:
blocks.explanation: At the top vf = 0 and g = -9.8 m s⁻². vf² - vi² = 2gh: 0 - 19.6² = 2(-9.8)h, so h = 19.6 m (2.5).

book_ref.quote: As regards the sign of g, it is taken positive for a falling body

blocks.prompt: 68 A ball thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m s⁻¹ reaches its highest point after:

book_ref.quote: According to Galileo, all bodies fall freely (in vacuum) under the acceleration due to gravity

blocks.prompt: 69 Projectile motion is:

options.text: two-dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity

blocks.explanation: The chapter defines projectile motion as two dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity (2.6).

book_ref.quote: Projectile motion is two dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity.

blocks.prompt: 70 Neglecting air resistance, the horizontal acceleration of a projectile is:
blocks.explanation: ax = 0 because air resistance is neglected and no force acts horizontally; ay = g (2.6).

book_ref.quote: The horizontal acceleration is ax = 0 because we have neglected air resistance

blocks.prompt: 71 A projectile is fired at 25 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Its horizontal velocity component during the flight is:

options.text: 12.5 m s⁻¹ at first, then decreasing

blocks.explanation: vfx = vix = vi cos θ = 25 × cos 60° = 12.5 m s⁻¹ and it stays constant (Eq. 2.18).

book_ref.quote: Hence, the horizontal component vix remains constant

blocks.prompt: 72 A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from a height of 19.6 m. It hits the ground after:
blocks.explanation: Vertical motion starts from zero: y = ½gt², so t = √(2 × 19.6/9.8) = 2 s (2.6). The horizontal speed does not change this time.

book_ref.quote: Since initial vertical velocity is zero, hence, vertical distance y, using Eq. 2.14 is given by

blocks.prompt: 73 For the ball thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from 19.6 m height, the horizontal distance covered before hitting the ground is:

book_ref.quote: The ball moves with constant horizontal velocity component.

blocks.prompt: 74 One ball is dropped and another is projected horizontally at the same instant from the same height. At any time:

options.text: both balls are at the same level
the projected ball has a larger vertical velocity

blocks.explanation: Their vertical displacements are equal at any time, so both are at the same level (2.6, Interesting Information).

book_ref.quote: At any time the two balls are at the same level

blocks.prompt: 75 A projectile is fired at 24 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Its vertical velocity component after 1 s is:
blocks.explanation: vfy = vi sin θ - gt = 24 × 0.5 - 9.8 × 1 = 12 - 9.8 = 2.2 m s⁻¹, still upward (Eq. 2.19).

book_ref.quote: considering the upward motion of projectile as free fall motion

blocks.prompt: 76 The angle φ that the velocity of a projectile makes with the horizontal at any instant is given by:
blocks.explanation: tan φ = vfy/vfx (Eq. 2.21), with v = √(vfx² + vfy²) (Eq. 2.20).

book_ref.quote: The angle φ which this resultant velocity makes with the horizontal can be found from

blocks.prompt: 77 At some instant a projectile has vfx = 15 m s⁻¹ and vfy = 19.6 m s⁻¹ downward. The magnitude of its velocity is about:

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of velocity at any instant is:

blocks.prompt: 78 The time taken by a projectile from the point of projection to the point where it hits the ground is called its:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of the time of flight (2.6).

book_ref.quote: The time taken by body to cover the distance from the place of its projection to the place where it hits the ground

blocks.prompt: 79 To find the time of flight of a projectile from level ground, the vertical displacement is taken as:
blocks.explanation: S = h = 0 because the body comes back to the same level (2.6).

book_ref.quote: This can be obtained by taking S = h = 0

blocks.prompt: 80 A ball is projected from the ground at 10 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Its time of flight is about:

book_ref.quote: Where t is the time of flight of the projectile when it is projected from the ground.

blocks.prompt: 81 A projectile is fired at 28 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. The maximum height it attains is:

book_ref.quote: In order to determine the maximum height the projectile attains, we use the equation of motion

blocks.prompt: 82 In the presence of air resistance, the maximum height of a projectile:
blocks.explanation: Air resistance decreases the upward velocity, so the height is reduced (2.6).

book_ref.quote: The height of projectile will be reduced in presence of air resistance.

blocks.prompt: 83 The maximum horizontal distance covered by a projectile is called its:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of the range of a projectile (2.6).

book_ref.quote: Maximum distance which a projectile covers in the horizontal direction is called the range of the projectile.

blocks.prompt: 84 The range of a projectile depends upon:

options.text: the mass of the projectile only
the velocity and the angle of projection

blocks.explanation: R = (vi²/g) sin 2θ, so the range depends on the velocity and the angle of projection (Eq. 2.24).

book_ref.quote: thus the range of the projectile depends upon the velocity of projection and the angle of projection

blocks.prompt: 85 The range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is:
blocks.explanation: Maximum range needs sin 2θ = 1, so 2θ = 90° and θ = 45° (2.6).

book_ref.quote: For maximum range R, the factor sin 2θ = 1, so

blocks.prompt: 86 A stone is projected at 14 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal from level ground. Its range is:

book_ref.quote: we multiply the horizontal component of the velocity of projection with total time taken by the body

blocks.prompt: 87 When a projectile is fired at an angle larger than 45° (same speed), compared with 45°:

options.text: the height and the range are both more
the height is more but the range is less
the height and the range are both less
the height is less but the range is more

blocks.explanation: Do You Know (2.6): above 45° the height attained is more but the range is less; below 45° both are less.

book_ref.quote: For an angle less than 45°, the height reached by the projectile and the range both will be less.

blocks.prompt: 88 Because of air resistance, the actual path of a high-speed projectile is:

options.text: skewed, with a steeper ascent than descent
skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent

blocks.explanation: Air resistance changes during the flight, so the trajectory is not perfectly parabolic but skewed, with steeper descent (2.6).

book_ref.quote: with steeper descent than ascent

blocks.prompt: 89 Air resistance reduces the range of a projectile mainly because it:

options.text: increases the mass of the projectile
reduces the velocity vi of the projectile

blocks.explanation: Air resistance slows the forward motion, reducing vi, and so the range decreases (2.6).

book_ref.quote: The reduction in vi will result in a decrease in the range of projectile.

blocks.prompt: 90 Newton called the quality of a moving body by which it exerts a force on anything that tries to stop it the:
blocks.explanation: Newton called it the quantity of motion; it is now called linear momentum (2.7).

book_ref.quote: This quality of the moving body was called the quantity of motion of the body, by Newton.

blocks.prompt: 91 Linear momentum is a vector quantity whose direction is that of the:
blocks.explanation: p = mv, so momentum is a vector with the direction of velocity (2.7).

book_ref.quote: Linear momentum is, therefore, a vector quantity and has the direction of velocity.

blocks.prompt: 92 The SI unit of momentum, kg m s⁻¹, can also be written as:
blocks.explanation: The SI unit of momentum is kg m s⁻¹, which can also be expressed as newton second (N s) (2.7).

book_ref.quote: It can also be expressed as newton second (N s).

blocks.prompt: 93 A 0.5 kg ball moves at 8 m s⁻¹. Its momentum is:
blocks.explanation: p = mv = 0.5 kg × 8 m s⁻¹ = 4 kg m s⁻¹ (Eq. 2.25).

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of momentum is kilogram metre per second

blocks.prompt: 94 The equation F × t = mvf - mvi shows that the change in momentum of a body equals the:

options.text: product of force and the time for which it acts

blocks.explanation: Eq. (2.26) shows that change in momentum is equal to the product of force and the time for which the force is applied (2.7).

book_ref.quote: shows that change in momentum is equal to the product of force and the time

blocks.prompt: 95 The momentum form of Newton's second law is more general than F = ma because it can also be applied when:

options.text: the mass of the body changes, as in a rocket
no force acts on the body
the body moves in a straight line

blocks.explanation: It can account for changes as the body accelerates while its mass also changes, e.g. a rocket losing mass (2.7).

book_ref.quote: This form of the second law is more general than the form F⃗ = ma⃗

blocks.prompt: 96 The product of the average force and the time for which it acts is called:
blocks.explanation: Impulse = F × t = mvf - mvi (Eq. 2.27).

book_ref.quote: The product of average force F that acts during time t is called impulse

blocks.prompt: 97 A bat exerts an average force of 200 N on a ball for 0.05 s. The impulse on the ball is:
blocks.explanation: Impulse = F × t = 200 N × 0.05 s = 10 N s (Eq. 2.27).

book_ref.quote: it is more convenient to deal with the product of force and time

blocks.prompt: 98 A 1200 kg car slows from 25 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. The average force on it is:
blocks.explanation: F = (mvf - mvi)/t = 1200 × (10 - 25)/5 = -3600 N; the negative sign shows a retarding force (Eq. 2.27).

book_ref.quote: The negative sign indicates that the force is retarding one.

blocks.prompt: 99 Kicking a stone (contact 1/100 s) hurts more than kicking a football (contact 1/10 s) with the same change in momentum because:

options.text: the shorter time means a larger force
the longer time means a larger force
impulse is zero for the stone

blocks.explanation: F = (mvf - mvi)/t: for the same change in momentum, a shorter time gives a larger force (2.7, Point to Ponder).

book_ref.quote: Which hurt you in the above situations (a) or (b) and think why?

blocks.prompt: 100 A motorcycle helmet is padded in order to:

options.text: shorten the time of a collision
increase the force on the head
extend the time of a collision and reduce the force

blocks.explanation: Padding extends the time of collision, so the force for the same change in momentum is smaller (2.7, Do You Know).

book_ref.quote: A motorcycle's safety helmet is padded so as to extend the time of any collision

blocks.prompt: 101 According to the chapter, a naked skull might fracture with about 5 N, but with skin and hair the force needed is about:
blocks.explanation: Hair acts like a crumple zone: 5 N may fracture the naked skull, but with skin and hair about 50 N would be needed (2.7, Do You Know).

book_ref.quote: Your hair acts like a crumple zone on your skull.

blocks.prompt: 102 A system on which no external agency exerts any force is called:
blocks.explanation: An isolated system is one on which no external agency exerts any force, e.g. gas molecules in a glass vessel (2.7).

book_ref.quote: It is a system on which no external agency exerts any force.

blocks.prompt: 103 The law of conservation of momentum states that the total linear momentum of an isolated system:
blocks.explanation: The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant (2.7).

book_ref.quote: The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant.

blocks.prompt: 104 In deriving the conservation of momentum for two colliding balls, the sum F + F′ is zero because:

options.text: action and reaction forces are equal and opposite
both forces act in the same direction
the balls move with equal velocities

blocks.explanation: F′ = -F (action and reaction), so F + F′ = 0 and the total change in momentum is zero (2.7).

book_ref.quote: Since the action force F⃗ is equal and opposite to the reaction force

blocks.prompt: 105 A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a 2 kg ball at rest. After the collision the 3 kg ball moves at 2 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. The velocity of the 2 kg ball is:

book_ref.quote: Consider an isolated system of two smooth hard interacting balls

blocks.prompt: 106 A 4 kg ball at 3 m s⁻¹ and a 2 kg ball at 6 m s⁻¹ move towards each other. The total momentum of the system is:
blocks.explanation: Momentum is a vector: 4 × 3 + 2 × (-6) = 12 - 12 = 0 (2.7).

book_ref.quote: In applying the conservation law, we must notice that the momentum of a body is a vector quantity.

blocks.prompt: 107 When a moving car stops quickly, passengers move forward. Seatbelts:

options.text: prevent the passengers from moving and reduce the chance of injury
increase the speed of the passengers
have no effect on the forces

blocks.explanation: Seatbelts change the forces of motion, prevent the passengers from moving and greatly reduce injury (2.7, Do You Know).

book_ref.quote: Seatbelts change the forces of motion and prevent the passengers from moving.

blocks.prompt: 108 A collision in which the kinetic energy of the system is not conserved is called:
blocks.explanation: When K.E. is not conserved the collision is inelastic (2.8).

book_ref.quote: A collision in which the K.E of the system is not conserved, is called inelastic collision.

blocks.prompt: 109 Which quantity is conserved only in elastic collisions?
blocks.explanation: Momentum and total energy are conserved in all collisions; K.E. is conserved only in elastic collisions (2.8).

book_ref.quote: However, the K.E. is conserved only in elastic collisions.

blocks.prompt: 110 A hard ball dropped on a marble floor rebounds very nearly to its initial height. The collision is nearly:

options.text: one in which momentum is lost
one in which all K.E. is lost

blocks.explanation: It loses a negligible amount of energy, so the collision is very nearly elastic (2.8).

book_ref.quote: it rebounds to very nearly the initial height

blocks.prompt: 111 When two tennis balls collide, part of the K.E. is lost partly due to friction as the molecules move past one another and partly due to:
blocks.explanation: Part of the K.E. is lost due to friction and partly due to its change into heat and sound (2.8).

book_ref.quote: partly due to its change into heat and sound energies

blocks.prompt: 112 In a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative velocity of approach is:

options.text: twice the relative velocity of separation
half the relative velocity of separation
equal in magnitude to the relative velocity of separation

blocks.explanation: (v1 - v2) = -(v1′ - v2′): the magnitude of relative velocity of approach equals that of separation (2.8).

book_ref.quote: the magnitude of relative velocity of approach is equal to the magnitude of relative velocity of separation

book_ref.quote: relative velocities before and after the collision has the same magnitude but are reversed

blocks.explanation: For m1 = m2 and v2 = 0: v1′ = 0 and v2′ = v1 (2.8, Fig. 2.12).

options.text: moves forward with twice the speed
bounces back with the same speed

blocks.explanation: For m2 >> m1 and v2 = 0: v1′ = -v1 and v2′ = 0; the squash player uses this (2.8, Fig. 2.13).

blocks.prompt: 120 A collision is two-dimensional when, after the collision, the bodies:

do not travel along the same initial axis

blocks.explanation: When bodies travelling along an axis do not end up travelling along the same axis after collision, the collision is two-dimensional (2.9).

blocks.prompt: 121 Two bodies colliding at a glancing angle shows that the collision is:
blocks.explanation: A glancing angle shows that the collision is not head-on (2.9).

m1v1f sin θ1 = m2v2f sin θ2

blocks.prompt: 123 In the equations of a 2D elastic collision with the target at rest, the number of unknown quantities is:
blocks.explanation: There are four unknowns, v1f, v2f, θ1 and θ2 (2.9).

book_ref.quote: there are four unknown quantities

blocks.prompt: 124 A bullet fired into a block of wood is an example of:

options.text: a collision with no loss of energy
a collision in which momentum is lost

blocks.explanation: Some energy of the bullet is lost as sound and heat, so the collision is inelastic (2.9, Interesting Information).

blocks.explanation: K.E.f = ½ × 1 × 4² + ½ × 1 × 3² = 8 + 4.5 = 12.5 J = K.E.i = ½ × 1 × 5², so K.E. is conserved (Eq. 2.36).

both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
